claim: Wnt signalling regulates multiple processes including angiogenesis, inflammation, and tumorigenesis.
source: Wnt signalling regulates multiple processes including angiogenesis, inflammation, and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Wnt signalling pathways.

claim: Norrin (Norrie Disease Protein) is a cystine-knot like growth factor.
source: Norrin (Norrie Disease Protein) is a cystine-knot like growth factor.
evidence: This is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript and established knowledge.

claim: Norrin is unrelated to Wnt.
source: Although unrelated to Wnt, Norrin activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural and evolutionary relationship between Norrin and Wnt.

claim: Norrin activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.
source: Although unrelated to Wnt, Norrin activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.
evidence: This is supported by the luciferase reporter assay data presented in the manuscript and prior literature.

claim: Signal complex formation involves Frizzled4 (Fz4), low-density lipoprotein receptor related protein 5/6 (Lrp5/6), Tetraspanin-12 and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs).
source: Signal complex formation involves Frizzled4 (Fz4), low-density lipoprotein receptor related protein 5/6 (Lrp5/6), Tetraspanin-12 and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: The study reports crystallographic analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD).
source: Here, we report crystallographic and small-angle X-ray scattering analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), of this complex bound with GAG analogues, and of unliganded Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data and structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study reports small-angle X-ray scattering analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4CRD.
source: Here, we report crystallographic and small-angle X-ray scattering analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), of this complex bound with GAG analogues, and of unliganded Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is directly supported by the SAXS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study reports analyses of the Norrin-Fz4CRD complex bound with GAG analogues.
source: Here, we report crystallographic and small-angle X-ray scattering analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), of this complex bound with GAG analogues, and of unliganded Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data showing SOS (sucrose octasulfate) binding.

claim: The study reports analyses of unliganded Norrin.
source: Here, we report crystallographic and small-angle X-ray scattering analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), of this complex bound with GAG analogues, and of unliganded Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data of Norrin alone.

claim: The study reports analyses of unliganded Fz4CRD.
source: Here, we report crystallographic and small-angle X-ray scattering analyses of Norrin in complex with Fz4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), of this complex bound with GAG analogues, and of unliganded Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data of Fz4CRD alone.

claim: Fz4 and putative Lrp5/6 binding sites map to distinct patches on Norrin.
source: Our structural, biophysical and cellular data, map Fz4 and putative Lrp5/6 binding sites to distinct patches on Norrin, and reveal a GAG binding site spanning Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data, mutagenesis studies, and binding assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: A GAG binding site spans Norrin and Fz4CRD.
source: Our structural, biophysical and cellular data, map Fz4 and putative Lrp5/6 binding sites to distinct patches on Norrin, and reveal a GAG binding site spanning Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing SOS binding and heparin binding assays.

claim: The results explain numerous disease-associated mutations.
source: These results explain numerous disease-associated mutations.
evidence: This is supported by mapping disease mutations onto the structures and showing their effects on binding and function.

claim: Norrin mimics Wnt for Frizzled recognition.
source: Comparison with the Xenopus Wnt8–mouse Fz8CRD complex reveals Norrin mimics Wnt for Frizzled recognition.
evidence: This is supported by structural superposition showing overlap of binding sites and structural similarity.

claim: Wnt morphogens are secreted cysteine-rich palmitoleoylated glycoproteins.
source: Wnt morphogens, secreted cysteine-rich palmitoleoylated glycoproteins, play critical roles in cell-fate determination, tissue homeostasis and embryonic development (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Malinauskas and Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wnt morphogens play critical roles in cell-fate determination, tissue homeostasis and embryonic development.
source: Wnt morphogens, secreted cysteine-rich palmitoleoylated glycoproteins, play critical roles in cell-fate determination, tissue homeostasis and embryonic development (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Malinauskas and Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Aberrant Wnt signalling leads to cancer, osteoporosis and degenerative illnesses.
source: Aberrant Wnt signalling leads to cancer, osteoporosis and degenerative illnesses (Anastas and Moon, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Norrie Disease Protein (NDP) gene encodes Norrin.
source: Norrie Disease Protein (NDP) gene encodes Norrin (Berger et al., 1992; Chen et al., 1992), a secreted cystine-knot like growth factor, distinct from the lipid-modified Wnt (Willert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Norrin is distinct from the lipid-modified Wnt.
source: Norrie Disease Protein (NDP) gene encodes Norrin (Berger et al., 1992; Chen et al., 1992), a secreted cystine-knot like growth factor, distinct from the lipid-modified Wnt (Willert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Norrin activates the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway by interaction with Wnt receptor Frizzled4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), and co-receptor low density lipoprotein receptor related protein 5/6 ectodomain (Lrp5/6ECD), plus the auxiliary four-pass transmembrane protein Tetraspanin-12 (Tspan-12) and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) of heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs).
source: Norrin activates the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway by interaction with Wnt receptor Frizzled4 cysteine-rich domain (Fz4CRD), and co-receptor low density lipoprotein receptor related protein 5/6 ectodomain (Lrp5/6ECD), plus the auxiliary four-pass transmembrane protein Tetraspanin-12 (Tspan-12) and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) of heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) (Xu et al., 2004; Junge et al., 2009; Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Norrin mediated pathway maintains the blood-retina and blood-brain barriers.
source: The Norrin mediated pathway maintains the blood-retina and blood-brain barriers (Wang et al., 2012) and regulates angiogenesis in the cochlea and uterus (Rehm et al., 2002; Ye et al., 2011) as well as neuroprotective effects on retinal neurons (Ohlmann et al., 2010; Seitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The Norrin mediated pathway regulates angiogenesis in the cochlea and uterus.
source: The Norrin mediated pathway maintains the blood-retina and blood-brain barriers (Wang et al., 2012) and regulates angiogenesis in the cochlea and uterus (Rehm et al., 2002; Ye et al., 2011) as well as neuroprotective effects on retinal neurons (Ohlmann et al., 2010; Seitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The Norrin mediated pathway has neuroprotective effects on retinal neurons.
source: The Norrin mediated pathway maintains the blood-retina and blood-brain barriers (Wang et al., 2012) and regulates angiogenesis in the cochlea and uterus (Rehm et al., 2002; Ye et al., 2011) as well as neuroprotective effects on retinal neurons (Ohlmann et al., 2010; Seitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in the NDP gene and the receptor genes, FZ4, LRP5, and TSPAN-12, have been identified for vitreoretinal diseases including Norrie Disease, Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy, and Coats' Disease.
source: Mutations in the NDP gene and the receptor genes, FZ4, LRP5, and TSPAN-12, have been identified for vitreoretinal diseases including Norrie Disease, Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy, and Coats' Disease (Nikopoulos et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2010; Ohlmann and Tamm, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: NDP, FZ4, LRP5, and TSPAN-12 knock-out mice experiments support the notion that dysfunctional Norrin signalling results in impaired retinal angiogenesis.
source: NDP, FZ4, LRP5, and TSPAN-12 knock-out mice experiments further support the notion that dysfunctional Norrin signalling results in impaired retinal angiogenesis (Richter et al., 1998; Kato et al., 2002; Robitaille et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2004; Junge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Norrin specifically binds to Fz4CRD, but not to the 14 other CRDs of Fz and secreted Frizzled-related protein (sFRP) family members.
source: Unlike Wnts which have promiscuous interactions with Fz receptors, Norrin specifically binds to Fz4CRD, but not to the 14 other CRDs of Fz and secreted Frizzled-related protein (sFRP) family members (Hsieh et al., 1999; Smallwood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations and the SPR data in this manuscript showing selective binding.

claim: Norrin binds to Lrp5/6ECD.
source: Similar to Wnt, Norrin (1) binds to Lrp5/6ECD (Ke et al., 2013); (2) interacts with HSPGs and shows limited spatial diffusion (Perez-Vilar and Hill, 1997; Xu et al., 2004; Smallwood et al., 2007; Ohlmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and SPR data in this manuscript.

claim: Norrin interacts with HSPGs and shows limited spatial diffusion.
source: Similar to Wnt, Norrin (1) binds to Lrp5/6ECD (Ke et al., 2013); (2) interacts with HSPGs and shows limited spatial diffusion (Perez-Vilar and Hill, 1997; Xu et al., 2004; Smallwood et al., 2007; Ohlmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and heparin binding data in this manuscript.

claim: Structural analyses of the extracellular components and interactions mediating Norrin signalling were considered to be challenging because of the difficulties of generating recombinant Norrin.
source: Structural analyses of the extracellular components and interactions mediating Norrin signalling were considered to be challenging because of the difficulties of generating recombinant Norrin (Perez-Vilar and Hill, 1997; Shastry and Trese, 2003; Ohlmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ke et al. (2013) reported a refolding method (from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies) to produce active recombinant Norrin fused with a N-terminal maltose binding protein (MBP-Norrin).
source: Ke et al. (2013) reported a refolding method (from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies) to produce active recombinant Norrin fused with a N-terminal maltose binding protein (MBP-Norrin), an advance that enabled them to determine the crystal structure of MBP-Norrin.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Ke et al. (2013) determined the crystal structure of MBP-Norrin.
source: Ke et al. (2013) reported a refolding method (from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies) to produce active recombinant Norrin fused with a N-terminal maltose binding protein (MBP-Norrin), an advance that enabled them to determine the crystal structure of MBP-Norrin.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: The study developed an efficient mammalian cell expression method to produce active untagged recombinant Norrin.
source: Here, we develop an efficient mammalian cell expression method to produce active untagged recombinant Norrin and detail the structural and functional properties of this potential therapeutic agent.
evidence: This is supported by the expression data and methods presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dimeric Norrin forms a complex with two copies of monomeric Fz4CRD.
source: Our crystallographic and solution studies further reveal that dimeric Norrin forms a complex with two copies of monomeric Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and SEC-MALS data showing 2:2 stoichiometry.

claim: Norrin uses its β-strands to mimic a finger-like loop in Wnt for binding to the Fz receptor CRD.
source: Structural comparison with the Xenopus Wnt8 in complex with mouse Fz8CRD (Janda et al., 2012) shows that Norrin uses its β-strands to mimic a finger-like loop in Wnt for binding to the Fz receptor CRD.
evidence: This is supported by structural superposition showing overlap of binding regions.

claim: Fusion of Norrin to the C-terminus of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) substantially boosted expression of the secreted protein in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells.
source: We found that fusion of Norrin to the C-terminus of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) (Peroutka et al., 2008), in combination with addition of valproic acid (Backliwal et al., 2008), a putative histone deacetylase inhibitor, substantially boosted expression of the secreted protein in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Addition of valproic acid substantially boosted expression of the secreted Norrin protein in HEK 293T cells.
source: We found that fusion of Norrin to the C-terminus of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) (Peroutka et al., 2008), in combination with addition of valproic acid (Backliwal et al., 2008), a putative histone deacetylase inhibitor, substantially boosted expression of the secreted protein in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After removal of the SUMO fusion tag, the recombinant Norrin shows a monodispersed state in size-exclusion chromatography.
source: After removal of the SUMO fusion tag, the recombinant Norrin shows a monodispersed state in size-exclusion chromatography (SEC; Figure 1D) and is biologically active in a cell-based luciferase reporter assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the SEC data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Recombinant Norrin is biologically active in a cell-based luciferase reporter assay.
source: After removal of the SUMO fusion tag, the recombinant Norrin shows a monodispersed state in size-exclusion chromatography (SEC; Figure 1D) and is biologically active in a cell-based luciferase reporter assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Three crystal structures of Norrin were determined.
source: We determined three crystal structures of Norrin (Figure 2A and Table 1), using selenomethionine-labeled protein for phasing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1 and structures shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Norrin protein fold is identical to that of the previously reported MBP-Norrin crystal structure.
source: The Norrin protein fold is identical to that of the previously reported MBP-Norrin crystal structure (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with the cited structure.

claim: Each Norrin monomer comprises three β-hairpins (β1-β2, β3-β4 and β5-β6), a β7 strand at the C-terminus, and four intramolecular disulphide bonds.
source: Each Norrin monomer comprises three β-hairpins (β1-β2, β3-β4 and β5-β6), a β7 strand at the C-terminus, and four intramolecular disulphide bonds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The two Norrin monomers assemble as an elongated, head-to-tail, dimer stabilized by three intermolecular disulphide bridges (Cys93-Cys95, Cys95-Cys93, and Cys131-Cys131).
source: The two monomers assemble as an elongated, head-to-tail, dimer (Figure 2A) stabilized by three intermolecular disulphide bridges (Cys93-Cys95, Cys95-Cys93, and Cys131-Cys131), in agreement with small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements which showed Norrin dimer in solution (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and SAXS data.

claim: SAXS measurements showed Norrin dimer in solution.
source: The two monomers assemble as an elongated, head-to-tail, dimer (Figure 2A) stabilized by three intermolecular disulphide bridges (Cys93-Cys95, Cys95-Cys93, and Cys131-Cys131), in agreement with small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements which showed Norrin dimer in solution (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Table 2.

claim: The Norrin dimer interface is stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
source: The dimer interface is further stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: Superposition of all molecules in the asymmetric units from the three crystal forms with the MBP-Norrin structure showed an average root-mean-square (r.m.s.) deviation of 1.5 Å over 190 equivalent Cα atoms.
source: Superposition of all molecules in the asymmetric units from our three crystal forms with the MBP-Norrin structure (Ke et al., 2013) showed an average root-mean-square (r.m.s.) deviation of 1.5 Å over 190 equivalent Cα atoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The β1-β2, β3-β4 and β5-β6 loops show a high degree of conformational plasticity.
source: On inspection the superpositions revealed a high degree of conformational plasticity in the β1-β2, β3-β4 and β5-β6 loops (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The flexibility in the β1-β2, β3-β4 and β5-β6 loop regions is consistent with the relatively high crystallographic B factor values.
source: The flexibility inherent in these regions is consistent with the relatively high crystallographic B factor values (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by B factor analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Disruption of the Norrin dimer by either Cysteine-to-Alanine mutations of intermolecular disulphide bonds or mutations of hydrophobic residues at the dimer interface results in a loss of Norrin-mediated signalling.
source: It has previously been noted that disruption of the dimer by either Cysteine-to-Alanine mutations of intermolecular disulphide bonds or mutations of hydrophobic residues at the dimer interface results in a loss of Norrin-mediated signalling (Smallwood et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two crystal structures of Fz4CRD were determined.
source: We determined two crystal structures of Fz4CRD (Figure 3 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1 and structures shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Fz4CRD fold comprises four α helices stabilized by five disulphide bridges (Cys45–Cys106, Cys53–Cys99, Cys90–Cys128, Cys117–Cys158, Cys121–Cys145).
source: Similar to mouse Fz8CRD (Dann et al., 2001) the Fz4CRD fold comprises four α helices (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) stabilized by five disulphide bridges (Cys45–Cys106, Cys53–Cys99, Cys90–Cys128, Cys117–Cys158, Cys121–Cys145).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The N-acetylglucosamines on two N-linked glycosylation sites at Asn59 and Asn144 are visible in the electron density map.
source: The N-acetylglucosamines on two N-linked glycosylation sites at Asn59 and Asn144 are visible in the electron density map (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Superposition of all Fz4CRD molecules in the asymmetric units from two crystal forms revealed a well-ordered protein fold.
source: Superposition of all Fz4CRD molecules in the asymmetric units from two crystal forms revealed a well-ordered protein fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy disease mutant C45Y results in misfolded protein retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy disease mutant C45Y results in misfolded protein retained in the endoplasmic reticulum, similar to the effects of Cysteine-to-Alanine mutations in the related CRD of Drosophila Smoothened (Smo) (Zhang et al., 2011; Rana et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fz4CRD closely resembles the CRDs of mouse Fz8 and secreted Frizzled-related protein 3 (sFRP3) with an average r.m.s. deviation of 1.2 Å over 115 equivalent Cα atoms.
source: Structural comparison showed Fz4CRD closely resembles the CRDs of mouse Fz8 and secreted Frizzled-related protein 3 (sFRP3) with an average r.m.s. deviation of 1.2 Å over 115 equivalent Cα atoms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E) and approximate sequence identity of 35%.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Fz4CRD has approximate sequence identity of 35% with mouse Fz8 and sFRP3 CRDs.
source: Structural comparison showed Fz4CRD closely resembles the CRDs of mouse Fz8 and secreted Frizzled-related protein 3 (sFRP3) with an average r.m.s. deviation of 1.2 Å over 115 equivalent Cα atoms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E) and approximate sequence identity of 35%.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison.

claim: Comparisons of Fz4CRD with the CRDs of muscle-specific kinase (MuSk) and Smo showed more substantial structural differences with an average r.m.s. deviation of 2.3 Å over 86 equivalent Cα atoms.
source: Comparisons with the CRDs of muscle-specific kinase (MuSk) and Smo showed more substantial structural differences with an average r.m.s. deviation of 2.3 Å over 86 equivalent Cα atoms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: SEC-MALS results showed Fz4CRD, Fz5CRD and Fz8CRD exist as monomers in solution at 50 μM concentration.
source: Size-exclusion chromatography coupled to multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) results (Figure 3B and Table 3) showed Fz4CRD, Fz5CRD and Fz8CRD exist as monomers in solution at 50 μM concentration, in agreement with previously reported SEC studies of Fz8CRD and SEC-MALS analyses of MuSKCRD and SmoCRD (Stiegler et al., 2009; Nachtergaele et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3B and Table 3.

claim: SAXS measurements support the conclusion that Fz4CRD is monomeric in solution at 290 μM concentration.
source: SAXS measurements further support the conclusion that Fz4CRD is monomeric in solution at 290 μM concentration (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The CRDs of Fz receptors exist as monomers and may not be involved in receptor dimerization.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the CRDs of Fz receptors exist as monomers and may not be involved in receptor dimerization; multiple GPCRs dimerize through their hepta-helical transmembrane domains (Rios et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC-MALS and SAXS data showing monomeric CRDs, and supported by citation about GPCR dimerization.

claim: The crystal structures of methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD and Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS were determined at 2.3 Å and 3.0 Å resolution, respectively.
source: We purified Norrin–Fz4CRD complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and determined the crystal structures of methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD (dimethylated surface-exposed lysine residues; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C) and Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS (complex bound with heparin mimic sucrose octasulfate, SOS; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) at 2.3 Å and 3.0 Å resolution, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD complex has a 2:1 stoichiometry.
source: These two complex structures show different stoichiometries: a 2:1 complex for the methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD and a 2:2:2 stoichiometry for the Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS complex, the architecture of which resembles a butterfly (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS complex has a 2:2:2 stoichiometry.
source: These two complex structures show different stoichiometries: a 2:1 complex for the methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD and a 2:2:2 stoichiometry for the Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS complex, the architecture of which resembles a butterfly (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Norrin–Fz4CRD binding interface is conserved between the complex structures.
source: The Norrin–Fz4CRD binding interface is conserved between the complex structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Each Fz4CRD interacts one-to-one with a separate Norrin chain, burying on average 1680 Å2 of surface area.
source: Each Fz4CRD interacts one-to-one with a separate Norrin chain, burying on average 1680 Å2 of surface area.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the complex.

claim: SEC-MALS shows Norrin interacts with Fz4CRD in a 2:2 stoichiometry.
source: To investigate the preference for complex formation in a 2:1 or 2:2 stoichiometry, we performed SEC-MALS (Figure 4B) and SAXS (Figure 4C) measurements in the absence of SOS. Both methods show Norrin interacts with Fz4CRD in a 2:2 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SAXS shows Norrin interacts with Fz4CRD in a 2:2 stoichiometry.
source: To investigate the preference for complex formation in a 2:1 or 2:2 stoichiometry, we performed SEC-MALS (Figure 4B) and SAXS (Figure 4C) measurements in the absence of SOS. Both methods show Norrin interacts with Fz4CRD in a 2:2 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lys102 and Lys104 are dimethylated in the uncomplexed subunit of the Norrin dimer in the methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD structure.
source: It is noteworthy that as Fc-dimerized Fz4CRD may mimic Fz4 receptor dimerization at the cellular surface, these tighter binding affinities may be more indicative of Norrin binding in the physiologically relevant environment.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 2:1 stoichiometry of methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD reflects the favourable crystallization characteristics of a sub population of asymmetrically methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD complexes.
source: This observation suggests that the 2:1 stoichiometry merely reflects the favourable crystallization characteristics of a sub population of asymmetrically methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of methylated lysines at the interface and the solution data showing 2:2 stoichiometry.

claim: The Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS structure defines the overall architecture of the native complex.
source: Thus although the methylated Norrin–Fz4CRD structure usefully provides high-resolution information for the ligand–receptor interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), the Norrin–Fz4CRD–SOS structure defines the overall architecture of the native complex (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the 2:2 stoichiometry observed in solution and the crystal structure.

claim: The two Fz4CRD diverge from the Norrin dimer without contacting each other.
source: The two Fz4CRD diverge from the Norrin dimer without contacting each other (Figure 4A), and with their C-termini suitably oriented for attachment to the same cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The C-termini of the two Fz4CRD are suitably oriented for attachment to the same cell surface.
source: The two Fz4CRD diverge from the Norrin dimer without contacting each other (Figure 4A), and with their C-termini suitably oriented for attachment to the same cell surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure showing the orientation of the C-termini.

claim: The Norrin–Fz4CRD complex has a novel architecture distinct from that of other cystine-knot secreted growth factors with either their receptors or antagonists.
source: The Norrin–Fz4CRD complex has a novel architecture; the mode of interaction of Norrin is distinct from that of other cystine-knot secreted growth factors (transforming growth factor-β, bone morphogenetic protein, platelet-derived growth factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor) with either their receptors or antagonists (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither Norrin nor Fz4CRD undergoes large conformational changes upon complex formation.
source: Neither Norrin nor Fz4CRD undergoes large conformational changes upon complex formation, although the flexibility of residues involved in the binding interface is reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The flexibility of residues involved in the Norrin-Fz4CRD binding interface is reduced upon complex formation.
source: Neither Norrin nor Fz4CRD undergoes large conformational changes upon complex formation, although the flexibility of residues involved in the binding interface is reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by B factor analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Superposition of the Norrin–Fz4CRD complex and the MBP-Norrin structure resulted in steric clashes between the Fz4CRD and the MBP.
source: Interestingly, superposition of the Norrin–Fz4CRD complex and the previously reported MBP-Norrin structure resulted in steric clashes between the Fz4CRD and the MBP (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural superposition shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: MBP hinders Norrin interaction with Fz4CRD.
source: This suggests that MBP hinders Norrin interaction with Fz4CRD consistent with MBP-Norrin only having half of the signalling activity of untagged Norrin (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the steric clashes observed and supported by citation showing reduced activity.

claim: MBP-Norrin has half of the signalling activity of untagged Norrin.
source: This suggests that MBP hinders Norrin interaction with Fz4CRD consistent with MBP-Norrin only having half of the signalling activity of untagged Norrin (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Two β-hairpins in Norrin (β1-β2 and β5-β6) contact three loops in Fz4CRD (I, II, and III) at the ligand–receptor interface.
source: At the ligand–receptor interface (Figure 5A) two β-hairpins in Norrin (β1-β2 and β5-β6) contact three loops in Fz4CRD (I, II, and III).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fz4CRD loop I hydrogen bonds to Norrin.
source: Fz4CRD loop I hydrogen bonds to Norrin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fz4CRD loop II makes extensive hydrophobic contacts plus one salt-bridge (Fz4CRD Lys109 with Norrin Asp46) with Norrin.
source: Fz4CRD loop II makes extensive hydrophobic contacts plus one salt-bridge (Fz4CRD Lys109 with Norrin Asp46; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fz4CRD loop III interacts with Norrin via an extensive hydrogen bond network as well as hydrophobic contacts.
source: Fz4CRD loop III interacts with Norrin via an extensive hydrogen bond network as well as hydrophobic contacts (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Interactions with SOS involve the positively charged residues of Lys58, Arg107, Arg109, and Arg115 on Norrin, plus His154 and Asn155 on Fz4CRD loop III.
source: Interactions with SOS involve the positively charged residues of Lys58, Arg107, Arg109, and Arg115 on Norrin, plus His154 and Asn155 on Fz4CRD loop III (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The residues Lys58, Arg107, Arg109, Arg115 on Norrin and His154, Asn155 on Fz4CRD define a likely binding site for GAGs.
source: These residues define a likely binding site for GAGs, in agreement with previous reports of Norrin interactions with extracellular matrix and heparin (Xu et al., 2004; Ohlmann et al., 2010).

claim: The Norrin–Fz4 interface revealed in the crystal structures is in excellent agreement with reported disease-associated mutations.
source: The Norrin–Fz4 interface revealed in our crystal structures (Figure 6A,B) is in excellent agreement with reported disease-associated mutations (Figure 6C) and surface residue conservation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by mapping disease mutations onto the structure shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Norrin–Fz4 interface is in excellent agreement with surface residue conservation.
source: The Norrin–Fz4 interface revealed in our crystal structures (Figure 6A,B) is in excellent agreement with reported disease-associated mutations (Figure 6C) and surface residue conservation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SPR experiments show a micromolar equilibrium dissociation constant between Norrin and Fz4CRD.
source: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiments (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) show a micromolar equilibrium dissociation constant between Norrin and Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutations of either H43N/V45T or L61N/A63S, which introduce an N-linked glycosylation site in the Fz4 binding site on Norrin, completely abolish the interaction with Fz4CRD.
source: Mutations of either H43N/V45T or L61N/A63S, which resulted in the introduction of an N-linked glycosylation site in the Fz4 binding site on Norrin, completely abolish the interaction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Norrin disease-associated mutants V45E and L61P/A63D lose binding affinity for Fz4CRD.
source: Norrin disease-associated mutants V45E and L61P/A63D lose binding affinity for Fz4CRD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), as do mutants R41E/H43E and R38E/R41S/H43E/K102E/K104E (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Norrin mutants R41E/H43E and R38E/R41S/H43E/K102E/K104E lose binding affinity for Fz4CRD.
source: Norrin disease-associated mutants V45E and L61P/A63D lose binding affinity for Fz4CRD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), as do mutants R41E/H43E and R38E/R41S/H43E/K102E/K104E (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Norrin mutants L52N/K54S and M114N/L116S show the same binding affinity as wild-type for Fz4CRD.
source: In contrast, Norrin mutants L52N/K54S and M114N/L116S (to introduce an N-linked glycosylation site in the β1-β2 loop or β5-β6 loop, respectively), predicted to lie outside the Fz4 binding site (Figure 6A), show the same binding affinity as wild-type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Cell-based Wnt/β-catenin responsive luciferase assays support the significance of the Fz4 binding site.
source: Cell-based Wnt/β-catenin responsive luciferase assays (Figure 6F) further support the significance of the Fz4 binding site.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Norrin mutants that lose binding to Fz4CRD fail to induce the luciferase reporter activity.
source: Norrin mutants that lose binding to Fz4CRD also fail to induce the luciferase reporter activity, in agreement with the SPR results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and prior genetic data (Xu et al., 2004; Smallwood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6F and SPR data.

claim: Norrin uses β strands (β1-β2 and β5-β6) for Fz4CRD binding.
source: Taken together, our structural and functional results suggest that Norrin uses β strands (β1-β2 and β5-β6) for Fz4CRD binding rather than, as proposed by Bazan et al. (2012) using the loop between β1 and β2 (Bazan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and mutagenesis data.

claim: Norrin has greatest affinity for Fz4CRD (Kd: 1 μM).
source: The results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) show that Norrin has greatest affinity for Fz4CRD (Kd: 1 μM), low affinities for Fz5CRD (Kd: 42 μM) and Fz8CRD (Kd: 64 μM), and no binding to Fz7CRD.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Norrin has low affinity for Fz5CRD (Kd: 42 μM).
source: The results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) show that Norrin has greatest affinity for Fz4CRD (Kd: 1 μM), low affinities for Fz5CRD (Kd: 42 μM) and Fz8CRD (Kd: 64 μM), and no binding to Fz7CRD.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Norrin has low affinity for Fz8CRD (Kd: 64 μM).
source: The results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) show that Norrin has greatest affinity for Fz4CRD (Kd: 1 μM), low affinities for Fz5CRD (Kd: 42 μM) and Fz8CRD (Kd: 64 μM), and no binding to Fz7CRD.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Norrin shows no binding to Fz7CRD.
source: The results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) show that Norrin has greatest affinity for Fz4CRD (Kd: 1 μM), low affinities for Fz5CRD (Kd: 42 μM) and Fz8CRD (Kd: 64 μM), and no binding to Fz7CRD.
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Pairing Norrin with Fz4CRD provides selective and high affinity binding relative to interactions with other CRD of Fz receptors.
source: In combination, these results confirm that pairing Norrin with Fz4CRD provides selective and high affinity binding relative to interactions with other CRD of Fz receptors, in agreement with prior studies (Xu et al., 2004; Smallwood et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data and citations.

claim: Norrin shows high affinity interaction with heparin.
source: Our heparin binding experiments confirmed that Norrin shows high affinity interaction with heparin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previous studies (Perez-Vilar and Hill, 1997; Xu et al., 2004; Smallwood et al., 2007; Ohlmann et al., 2010), and further demonstrated Norrin–Fz4CRD complex binding to heparin (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by heparin affinity chromatography data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Norrin–Fz4CRD complex binds to heparin.
source: Our heparin binding experiments confirmed that Norrin shows high affinity interaction with heparin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previous studies (Perez-Vilar and Hill, 1997; Xu et al., 2004; Smallwood et al., 2007; Ohlmann et al., 2010), and further demonstrated Norrin–Fz4CRD complex binding to heparin (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by heparin affinity chromatography data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Norrin triple mutation R107E/R109E/R115L impaired heparin binding.
source: The Norrin triple mutation R107E/R109E/R115L (R115L is a disease-associated mutation; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) impaired heparin binding (Figure 7B) and abolished signalling activity (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by heparin affinity chromatography data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Norrin triple mutation R107E/R109E/R115L abolished signalling activity.
source: The Norrin triple mutation R107E/R109E/R115L (R115L is a disease-associated mutation; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) impaired heparin binding (Figure 7B) and abolished signalling activity (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Norrin R107E/R109E/R115L mutant retained the ability to bind Fz4CRD.
source: However, this mutant protein retained the ability to bind Fz4CRD (Figure 7D) with a 2:2 stoichiometry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The Norrin R107E/R109E/R115L mutant binds Fz4CRD with a 2:2 stoichiometry.
source: However, this mutant protein retained the ability to bind Fz4CRD (Figure 7D) with a 2:2 stoichiometry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both wild-type and R107E/R109E/R115L mutant Norrin bind to Lrp6P1E1P2E2.
source: Ke et al. (2013) have reported MBP-Norrin binding to the Lrp6 ectodomain fragment comprising the first two tandem β-propeller-epidermal growth factor-like domain pairs (Lrp6P1E1P2E2; Ke et al., 2013); we found both our wild-type and R107E/R109E/R115L mutant Norrin bind to Lrp6P1E1P2E2 (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: The Norrin K58N mutant exhibited half of wild-type activity in the cell-based assay.
source: The Norrin K58N mutant (a disease-associated mutation; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) exhibited half of wild-type activity in our cell-based assay (Figure 7C), but did not affect Fz4CRD interaction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Norrin K58N mutant did not affect Fz4CRD interaction.
source: The Norrin K58N mutant (a disease-associated mutation; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) exhibited half of wild-type activity in our cell-based assay (Figure 7C), but did not affect Fz4CRD interaction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Residues Arg107, Arg109, and Arg115 are involved in GAG binding rather than Lrp5/6 binding.
source: These results are in agreement with previous functional studies (Smallwood et al., 2007), and suggest this area is a GAG binding site rather than that, as Ke et al. (2013) proposed, residues Arg107, Arg109, and Arg115 are involved in Lrp5/6 binding (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing loss of heparin binding but retention of Lrp6 binding.

claim: HSPGs play important roles in the regulation of the Wnt signalling pathway.
source: HSPGs play important roles in the regulation of the Wnt signalling pathway (Malinauskas and Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Wnt signalling activity can be inhibited by treatment with exogenous heparin.
source: Wnt signalling activity can be inhibited by treatment with exogenous heparin (Ai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: PG545, a heparan sulphate mimetic, can block Wnt binding to the cell surface and inhibit Wnt signalling.
source: Also, Jung et al. (2015) have reported that PG545, a heparan sulphate mimetic, can block Wnt binding to the cell surface, by competing with endogenous HSPGs, and inhibit Wnt signalling (Jung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: SOS could inhibit Norrin mediated Wnt/β-catenin signalling activity when pre-incubated with Norrin before stimulation of reporter cells.
source: For Norrin mediated Wnt/β-catenin signalling, we found that SOS could inhibit activity when pre-incubated with Norrin before stimulation of reporter cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Five residues (Lys54, Arg90, Arg97, Gly112, and Arg121) form a continuous, positively charged, concave patch on Norrin that is a potential Lrp5/6 binding site.
source: To identify Norrin residues potentially involved in Lrp5/6ECD binding, we assessed solvent exposure, disease-association, and lack of involvement in Fz4CRD or GAG binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Five residues (Lys54, Arg90, Arg97, Gly112, and Arg121) were highlighted by this analysis and form a continuous, positively charged, concave patch (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and disease mutation mapping shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A negatively charged region of the Lrp6ECD surface has been implicated in ligand binding.
source: Notably, a negatively charged region of the Lrp6ECD surface has been implicated in ligand binding (Ahn et al., 2011; Bourhis et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The disease-associated Norrin mutant R121W substantially impairs signalling activity.
source: To test our proposed location for the Lrp5/6 binding site, we generated the disease-associated Norrin mutant R121W (Arg121 is a mutational hotspot; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This mutation substantially impairs signalling activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), but retains the ability to interact with Fz4CRD (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and heparin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Norrin R121W mutant retains the ability to interact with Fz4CRD.
source: To test our proposed location for the Lrp5/6 binding site, we generated the disease-associated Norrin mutant R121W (Arg121 is a mutational hotspot; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This mutation substantially impairs signalling activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), but retains the ability to interact with Fz4CRD (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and heparin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Norrin R121W mutant retains the ability to interact with heparin.
source: To test our proposed location for the Lrp5/6 binding site, we generated the disease-associated Norrin mutant R121W (Arg121 is a mutational hotspot; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This mutation substantially impairs signalling activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), but retains the ability to interact with Fz4CRD (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and heparin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by heparin affinity chromatography data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The R121W mutation reduced Norrin protein solubility and stability during protein production and in heparin binding assays.
source: However, we found the R121W mutation reduced protein solubility and stability during protein production and in heparin binding assays.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work.

claim: Norrin has three distinct and independent binding sites for Fz4, Lrp5/6, and GAGs.
source: Taken together, the current data suggest three distinct and independent binding sites on Norrin for Fz4, Lrp5/6, and GAGs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and mutagenesis data showing separate binding sites.

claim: The arrangement of binding sites on Norrin likely enables Norrin to form a ternary complex.
source: This arrangement of binding sites likely enables Norrin to form a ternary complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial arrangement of binding sites.

claim: Xenopus Wnt8 uses 'thumb' and 'index finger' regions to grasp mouse Fz8CRD at two distinct sites.
source: Xenopus Wnt8 (Figure 9A) has been described as using 'thumb' and 'index finger' regions to grasp mouse Fz8CRD at two distinct sites (Janda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: A palmitoleoyl group (PAM) covalently linked to the tip of the Wnt8 thumb inserts into a groove in Fz8CRD at site 1.
source: In site 1, a palmitoleoyl group (PAM) covalently linked to the tip of the thumb inserts into a groove in Fz8CRD, removal of this PAM moiety suppresses Wnt signalling activity (Kakugawa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Removal of the PAM moiety from Wnt8 suppresses Wnt signalling activity.
source: In site 1, a palmitoleoyl group (PAM) covalently linked to the tip of the thumb inserts into a groove in Fz8CRD, removal of this PAM moiety suppresses Wnt signalling activity (Kakugawa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The Wnt8 index finger contacts a hydrophobic pocket on Fz8CRD at site 2.
source: In site 2, the index finger contacts a hydrophobic pocket.
evidence: This is supported by the cited Wnt8-Fz8CRD structure.

claim: There are no major structural differences between Fz4CRD and Fz8CRD (r.m.s. deviation of 1.3 Å over 110 equivalent Cα atoms).
source: We superposed Norrin–Fz4CRD with Wnt8–Fz8CRD. There are no major structural differences between the Fz4CRD and Fz8CRD (r.m.s. deviation of 1.3 Å over 110 equivalent Cα atoms; Figure 9A), and the structural elements that mediate site 1 PAM binding in Fz8CRD are largely conserved in Fz4CRD (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The structural elements that mediate site 1 PAM binding in Fz8CRD are largely conserved in Fz4CRD.
source: We superposed Norrin–Fz4CRD with Wnt8–Fz8CRD. There are no major structural differences between the Fz4CRD and Fz8CRD (r.m.s. deviation of 1.3 Å over 110 equivalent Cα atoms; Figure 9A), and the structural elements that mediate site 1 PAM binding in Fz8CRD are largely conserved in Fz4CRD (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The Norrin binding site on Fz4CRD overlaps with site 2 on Fz8CRD.
source: The Norrin binding site on Fz4CRD (∼800 Å2 buried area) overlaps with site 2 on Fz8CRD (∼400 Å2 buried area; Figure 8A), in agreement with previous mutational mapping studies (Smallwood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9A and citation.

claim: The position of the Wnt8 index finger overlaps with Norrin β1 and β2.
source: The position of the Wnt8 index finger overlaps with Norrin β1 and β2, and, unexpectedly, these β strands show some structural equivalence with Wnt8 (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Norrin β1 and β2 strands show some structural equivalence with the Wnt8 index finger.
source: The position of the Wnt8 index finger overlaps with Norrin β1 and β2, and, unexpectedly, these β strands show some structural equivalence with Wnt8 (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Site 2 Wnt8 residues are strictly conserved in all Wnts.
source: Site 2 Wnt8 residues are strictly conserved in all Wnts, and the apolar residues in the corresponding positions on Norrin are associated with disease mutations (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The apolar residues in the corresponding positions on Norrin to site 2 Wnt8 residues are associated with disease mutations.
source: Site 2 Wnt8 residues are strictly conserved in all Wnts, and the apolar residues in the corresponding positions on Norrin are associated with disease mutations (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by disease mutation mapping shown in Figure 9C.

claim: In Fz4CRD loop I, Asn55 is replaced by Fz8CRD Gly45, a change that would abolish interaction with Norrin Ser34.
source: In Fz4CRD loop I (Figure 9D), Asn55 is replaced by Fz8CRD Gly45, a change that would abolish interaction with Norrin Ser34 in the complex (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 9D.

claim: In Fz4CRD loop II, the substitution of Lys109 by Fz8CRD Asp99 would introduce an unfavorable electrostatic interaction with Norrin Asp46.
source: In Fz4CRD loop II (Figure 9E), the substitution of Lys109 by Fz8CRD Asp99 would introduce an unfavorable electrostatic interaction with Norrin Asp46 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 9E.

claim: In Fz4CRD loop III, hydrogen bonds and salt bridges to Norrin would be lost on replacing Asn152 and Glu160 with Fz8CRD Gly142 and Asp150 respectively.
source: Thirdly, in Fz4CRD loop III (Figure 9F), hydrogen bonds and salt bridges to Norrin would be lost on replacing Asn152 and Glu160 with Fz8CRD Gly142 and Asp150 respectively (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The residue substitutions between Fz4CRD and Fz8CRD have been reported to affect Fz4CRD binding to Norrin.
source: Consistent with this analysis, these residue substitutions have been reported to affect Fz4CRD binding to Norrin (Smallwood et al., 2007), and Fz4CRD is unique in containing this particular combination of residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Fz4CRD is unique in containing the particular combination of residues that enable Norrin binding.
source: Consistent with this analysis, these residue substitutions have been reported to affect Fz4CRD binding to Norrin (Smallwood et al., 2007), and Fz4CRD is unique in containing this particular combination of residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A GAG binding site may span Norrin and Fz4CRD.
source: Overall, our analyses provide several advances for our understanding of Norrin and Wnt signalling. Firstly, our results give fresh insight into the role of HSPGs. HSPGs have been proposed to regulate the local distribution of ligand and receptor at the cell surface, potentially acting as an introductory agency for ligand and receptor (Lin and Perrimon, 1999; Baeg et al., 2001; Malinauskas et al., 2011; Malinauskas and Jones, 2014). We have discovered a GAG binding site that may span Norrin and Fz4CRD (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing SOS binding across both proteins.

claim: The binding affinity of Norrin with Fz4CRD is enhanced in the presence of heparin.
source: Interestingly, Smallwood et al. (2007) found the binding affinity of Norrin with Fz4CRD is enhanced in the presence of heparin (Smallwood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The extended GAG binding site may allow co-receptor HSPGs to recruit secreted Norrin for interaction with Fz4CRD and to co-localize Norrin and Fz4 receptor.
source: We propose that the extended GAG binding site may allow co-receptor HSPGs to recruit secreted Norrin for interaction with Fz4CRD and to co-localize Norrin and Fz4 receptor, similar to the role of HSPGs in Wnt signalling (Reichsman et al., 1996; Baeg et al., 2001; Fuerer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural data and supported by citations about HSPG roles.

claim: HSPGs regulate the Wnt morphogenetic gradient.
source: For example, HSPGs have been shown to regulate the Wnt morphogenetic gradient (Lin and Perrimon, 1999; Baeg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Fz4CRD binds to the GAGs of the human HSPG Glypican-3.
source: Also, Capurro et al. (2014) have reported that Fz4CRD binds to the GAGs of the human HSPG Glypican-3 and that these interactions are involved in Wnt signal complex formation (Capurro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Fz4CRD-Glypican-3 interactions are involved in Wnt signal complex formation.
source: Also, Capurro et al. (2014) have reported that Fz4CRD binds to the GAGs of the human HSPG Glypican-3 and that these interactions are involved in Wnt signal complex formation (Capurro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The Norrin dimer binds separately to two molecules of Fz4CRD, in contrast to the 1:1 complex of Wnt8–Fz8CRD.
source: Secondly, we show the Norrin dimer binds separately to two molecules of Fz4CRD (Figure 4), in contrast to the 1:1 complex of Wnt8–Fz8CRD (Janda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and solution data.

claim: The discovery of the Fz4 and GAG binding sites, and analysis of a potential Lrp5/6 binding region, maps out distinct binding surfaces on Norrin.
source: Our discovery of the Fz4 and GAG binding sites, and analysis of a potential Lrp5/6 binding region, maps out distinct binding surfaces on Norrin (Figure 8B), which provide a framework in which to understand the effects of inherited mutations and probe the overall architecture of the ternary complex (Norrin–Fz4CRD–Lrp5/6ECD).
evidence: This is supported by the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: Norrin structurally mimics Wnt for site 2 binding surfaces on the Fz ectodomain.
source: Thirdly, we determine how Norrin structurally mimics Wnt for site 2 binding surfaces on the Fz ectodomain (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Site 2 binding to the CRD of Fz receptors can activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling albeit weakly.
source: Interestingly, previous analyses using water-soluble 'mini-Wnt' proteins, which cannot contribute site 1 binding, have raised the possibility that site 2 binding to the CRD of Fz receptors can activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling albeit weakly (Janda et al., 2012; von Maltzahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The site 2 binding mode is central to signallosome formation for Norrin mediated signalling.
source: Our findings indicate that the site 2 binding mode is central to signallosome formation for Norrin mediated signalling.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing Norrin mimics Wnt at site 2.

claim: The Kd value of 1.1 μM for the interaction between Norrin and Fz4CRD is weaker than previously published results.
source: We used SPR experiments to establish the binding affinity for Norrin–Fz4CRD complex formation. The Kd value of 1.1 μM for the interaction between Norrin and Fz4CRD we report here (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) is weaker than previously published results (Xu et al., 2004; Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited prior work.

claim: The discrepancy in Kd values is likely due to SPR binding assays being carried out with monomeric Fz4CRD.
source: This discrepancy is likely due to our SPR binding assays being carried out with monomeric Fz4CRD.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design.

claim: Xu et al. (2004) reported an affinity of 3–4 nM for mouse Norrin fused with C-terminal alkaline phosphatase binding to mouse Fz4CRD dimerized by a C-terminal Fc fusion.
source: Xu et al. (2004) used an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay to give an affinity of 3–4 nM for mouse Norrin fused with C-terminal alkaline phosphatase binding to mouse Fz4CRD dimerized by a C-terminal Fc fusion (Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Ke et al. (2013) reported Kd values of 11 nM and 5 nM for the interaction between MBP-Norrin and Fc-tagged dimeric Fz4CRD.
source: Ke et al. (2013) reported Kd values of 11 nM and 5 nM for the interaction between MBP-Norrin and Fc-tagged dimeric Fz4CRD using an AlphaScreen luminescence assay and biolayer interferometry, respectively (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Fc-dimerized Fz4CRD may mimic Fz4 receptor dimerization at the cellular surface.
source: It is noteworthy that as Fc-dimerized Fz4CRD may mimic Fz4 receptor dimerization at the cellular surface, these tighter binding affinities may be more indicative of Norrin binding in the physiologically relevant environment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental design.

claim: The Kd value of 2.87 μM for Norrin binding to Lrp6P1E1P2E2 differs from the Kd value of 0.45 μM reported by Ke et al. (2013).
source: Similarly, our Kd value of 2.87 μM for Norrin binding to Lrp6P1E1P2E2 in an SPR based assay (Figure 7E) differs from the Kd value of 0.45 μM reported by Ke et al. (2013) based on an homologous AlphaScreen competition assay using unlabeled MBP-Norrin against biotinylated MBP-Norrin for interaction with Lrp6P1E1P2E2 (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited prior work.

claim: The studies are consistent with Norrin-induced receptor clustering and signallosome formation.
source: Our studies reported here, in combination with previous findings for Norrin and Wnt signalling, are consistent with Norrin-induced receptor clustering and signallosome formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and prior knowledge.

claim: Inactive pre-dimerized Fz4 may engage with homodimeric Tspan-12 to enhance receptor clustering.
source: Inactive pre-dimerized Fz4 may engage with homodimeric Tspan-12 to enhance receptor clustering (Kaykas et al., 2004; Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Norrin binding generates ternary complex formation by Fz4, Lrp5/6 and the GAGs of HSPGs to trigger signalling, which is enhanced in the presence of Tspan12.
source: Norrin binding generates ternary complex formation by Fz4, Lrp5/6 and the GAGs of HSPGs to trigger signalling, which is enhanced in the presence of Tspan12.
